summary: A culture columnist recounts a series of encounters in autumn 2023, beginning in the town of Wakanda Lake, with Indigenous artists who keep traditional techniques alive and extend them into new forms. The pieces cover beadwork, basketry, painting, woodcarving, mixed-media textiles, digital art and pottery, and each artist describes art as heritage, story and resilience. The columnist presents this as a renaissance, boosted by the Indigenous Contemporary Art Fair on September 15, 2023.
one_line: A columnist's autumn 2023 tour of Indigenous artists across basketry, painting, carving, textiles, digital art and pottery shows traditional techniques thriving as storytelling.
key_facts: The columnist's encounter in the workshop at Wakanda Lake took place on a crisp October morning in 2023.
Interest in Indigenous art surged after the landmark Indigenous Contemporary Art Fair on September 15, 2023.
James Two Elk is a Dakota beadworker whose designs tell his ancestors' stories; he said, "It's not just art. It's heritage, it's history, and it's a narrative of resilience."
Ellen Blackbird, of the Salish people, weaves baskets; the columnist met her on September 20, 2023, and she said, "Each pattern has a tale."
In Salish basketry, triangular shapes represent mountains and circular motifs reflect the cyclical paths of the seasons and life.
Haida painter Jonathan White Bear uses pigments from natural minerals and plants; the columnist saw his exhibition on October 3, 2023.
Navajo carver Michael Yazzie was visited on October 23, 2023; his carvings draw on the Navajo creation legend and use cedar and pine.
Aniyunwiya textile artist Sarah Running Wolf blends traditional Cherokee weaving with contemporary materials such as synthetic fibers; her show was on November 5, 2023.
Mia Grey Owl and Jason Little Hawk launched the "Ancestral Pixels" collection on December 2, 2023, turning Indigenous iconography into digital art that can be taken into virtual reality.
On December 14, 2023, the columnist joined a hands-on traditional Pueblo pottery workshop led by potter David Whitefeather.
David Whitefeather said, "Clay is the journal of the earth. We're just writing our stories into it."
The article argues Indigenous art has moved from being neglected to the forefront of an emerging renaissance.
